The golden-collared toucanet (Selenidera reinwardtii) exhibits a fascinating suite of life-history traits that reflect its ecological niche as a frugivorous inhabitant of Neotropical forests. Newly hatched nestlings are altricial, emerging from incubated eggs at a remarkably small size; based on data from the closely related Selenidera piperivora, the initial wet weight of a neonate is just 7.1 grams [Ww0 = 7.1 grams], a minimal mass that underscores the heavy reliance on parental provisioning during early development. This altricial chick requires an incubation period of approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days] at a stable nest temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a duration that aligns with the relatively short incubation times observed in other small ramphastids. Following hatching, the nestling undergoes rapid somatic growth, gaining mass steadily as it is repeatedly fed by both parents. The substantial investment in post-hatching care is reflected in the developmental timeline: under the thermal conditions typical of an adult's active metabolic state (41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]), the fledgling achieves independence at roughly 42 days after hatching [tx = roughly 42 days after hatching], a benchmark that marks the transition to self-foraging.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a protracted trajectory, with reproductive organs developing gradually over several months. At a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], representing normothermic conditions, individuals are estimated to reach puberty at approximately 126 days after hatching [tp = approximately 126 days after hatching]. This rather late onset of gonadal maturity for a bird of its size suggests that considerable energy is first allocated to achieving a definitive adult body structure. The slow life pace is further evidenced by the maximum recorded longevity; field studies and captive records indicate that the most enduring individuals can survive for 13 years [am = 13 years] under optimal conditions, a lifespan that is relatively long compared to other small-bodied Neotropical passerines at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The first successful reproductive event does not occur immediately upon reaching sexual maturity; instead, first breeding is typically deferred until about 365 days after hatching [tR = about 365 days after hatching] at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], indicating a period during which young adults continue to refine foraging skills and establish a territory.

Considerable sexual dimorphism in body mass is evident in adults, a trait common among ramphastids. Females attain a maximum adult body mass of 156.75 grams [Wwi = 156.75 grams], whereas males are significantly heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 176 grams [Wwi = 176 grams]. This difference of nearly 20 grams likely reflects divergent selective pressures, with males potentially requiring greater mass for competitive interactions over nest cavities or foraging resources, while females may benefit from a lighter frame during the energetically demanding incubation and brooding periods. Basal metabolic rate for this species was measured under controlled laboratory conditions. At a thermoneutral temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption recorded was 218.18 milliliters per hour [JOi = 218.18 milliliters per hour], a value that scales appropriately with the species' moderate body size and frugivorous diet, which typically requires a relatively low metabolic intensity compared to insectivorous birds of similar mass. This rate provides a baseline for understanding daily energetic expenditures.

Reproductive output in the golden-collared toucanet is modest, consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity. Females typically lay 2 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 4 eggs per clutch], a relatively small brood size that allows for intensive biparental care of the altricial young. Furthermore, the species is single-brooded, with pairs producing just 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year]. This low annual fecundity, combined with the long developmental periods and extended lifespan, places Selenidera reinwardtii firmly on the slow end of the life-history continuum among Neotropical birds. The energetic investment per offspring is substantial, as each egg and subsequent nestling requires significant provisioning of fruit and occasional arthropods. The combination of a limited clutch size and a single annual breeding attempt means that population growth rates are inherently slow, making the species potentially vulnerable to habitat fragmentation or increased nest predation rates in degraded landscapes.

Comparative analyses within the Ramphastidae family reveal that the golden-collared toucanet's life-history parameters are generally consistent with those of other small-bodied members of the genus Selenidera. For instance, the ultimate wet weight of males, recorded at 176 grams [Wwi = 176 grams], is comparable to that of the closely related Selenidera gouldii. The maximum lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] falls within the range reported for captive Ramphastidae, which can live for over a decade under managed care at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The age at first breeding has been observed at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], which represents a full year dedicated to maturation and territory establishment. The development of the young remains a critical phase; fledging occurs at 42 days after hatching [tx = 42 days after hatching] in the same thermal regime, after which juvenile birds begin to explore independently at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. Puberty at 126 days after hatching [tp = 126 days after hatching] at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] marks the attainment of reproductive potential, though full adult mass and breeding readiness may take further months to achieve fully.
